current_text: Renoir spent about three years (1884-87) on The Large Bathers, now in Philadelphia, basing it partly on Girardon's 1672 lead relief The Bath of the Nymphs at Versailles.
new_text: Renoir spent about three years (1884-87) on The Large Bathers, now in Philadelphia, basing it partly on Girardon's 1672 lead relief The Bath of the Nymphs at Versailles.
source_note: Philadelphia Museum object page (titled 'The Great Bathers'): 1884-1887, 'labored over this work for three years'. Girardon's Bain des nymphes at Versailles as source confirmed by Smarthistory (smarthistory.org/auguste-renoir-the-large-bathers), not on the museum page; '1672' and 'lead' not confirmed by either.

current_text: Pissarro was the only artist to show at all eight Paris Impressionist exhibitions, from 1874 to 1886.
new_text: Pissarro was the only artist to show at all eight Paris Impressionist exhibitions, from 1874 to 1886.
source_note: Britannica: eight exhibitions 1874-1886; Pissarro the only artist who exhibited in all eight (Morisot in seven).

current_text: In 1874, the year of the first Impressionist show, Berthe Morisot married Eugene Manet, younger brother of Edouard Manet, who had painted her many times.
new_text: In 1874, the year of the first Impressionist show, Berthe Morisot married Eugene Manet, younger brother of Edouard Manet, who had painted her many times.
source_note: Britannica: in 1874 Morisot married Manet's younger brother Eugene; Edouard painted a series of portraits of her until the marriage (also Orsay 'Berthe Morisot, modele d'Edouard Manet').

current_text: Born in Paris to a British merchant father, Sisley stayed British all his life: his 1898 application for French citizenship was refused and a second was overtaken by his final illness.
new_text: Born in Paris to a British merchant father, Sisley stayed British all his life: his 1898 application for French citizenship was refused and a second was overtaken by his final illness.
source_note: Musee d'Orsay and National Gallery artist pages confirm only Paris birth to British parents / British nationality; no stronger source found for the 1898 refusal and second application.

current_text: Cassatt's The Child's Bath (1893, Art Institute of Chicago) followed her study of the 1890 Paris exhibition of Japanese prints: high viewpoint, flat patterns, cropped figures.
new_text: Cassatt's The Child's Bath (1893, Art Institute of Chicago) followed her study of the 1890 Paris exhibition of Japanese prints: high viewpoint, flat patterns, cropped figures.
source_note: Art Institute: 1893; Cassatt saw the large 1890 Japanese print exhibition at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts; painting is the culmination of her flattened picture plane and decorative patterning. 'High viewpoint' and 'cropped figures' not stated verbatim.

current_text: Cassatt urged her friend Louisine Havemeyer to buy her first artwork, a Degas pastel; the Havemeyer bequest after 1929 gave the Met nearly 2,000 works.
new_text: Cassatt urged her friend Louisine Havemeyer to buy her first artwork, a Degas pastel; the Havemeyer bequest after 1929 gave the Met nearly 2,000 works.
source_note: Met: 1929 Havemeyer bequest of nearly 2,000 objects; Met Cassatt audio transcript: Cassatt guided the collection and Louisine called her its 'fairy godmother'. The specific first purchase (a Degas pastel) not confirmed by the Met pages found.

current_text: Caillebotte bought his first Monet in 1875, paid studio rents for friends, and in 1877 secured the rooms at 6 rue Le Peletier, chose the artists and hung the third Impressionist show himself.
new_text: Caillebotte bought his first Monet in 1875, paid studio rents for friends, and in 1877 secured the rooms at 6 rue Le Peletier, chose the artists and hung the third Impressionist show himself.
source_note: Art Institute of Chicago: for the 1877 show on rue Le Peletier he found and rented the space, decided which artists to include and helped hang the paintings. 'First Monet in 1875', 'paid studio rents' and street number 6 not confirmed.

current_text: Bazille died in 1870, before any Impressionist show; instead he kept Monet afloat by buying Women in the Garden for 2,500 francs, paid in monthly instalments of 50 francs.
new_text: Bazille died in 1870, before any Impressionist show; instead he kept Monet afloat by buying Women in the Garden for 2,500 francs, paid in monthly instalments of 50 francs.
source_note: Fondation Napoleon: Bazille bought it for 2,500 francs payable in instalments of 50 francs, to support Monet; Orsay object page confirms it entered Bazille's collection (May 1867). 'Monthly' not stated explicitly.

current_text: In 1891 Guillaumin won 100,000 francs in the French state lottery, quit his government job and painted full-time.
new_text: Late in 1891 Guillaumin won 100,000 francs in a Credit Foncier bond lottery, quit his government job and painted full-time.
source_note: Museo Thyssen: late 1891, 100,000 francs from a Credit Foncier bond lottery. Britannica instead says 1892 and a 'city lottery' (also confirms quitting the government job). Year disputed between sources; amount consistent.

current_text: The barmaid in Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère (Salon 1882) was Suzon, a real Folies employee posed in his studio; the canvas first hung above Emmanuel Chabrier's piano.
new_text: The barmaid in Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère (Salon 1882) was Suzon, a real Folies employee posed in his studio; the canvas first hung above Emmanuel Chabrier's piano.
source_note: Courtauld: painted entirely in the studio where a barmaid named Suzon came to pose; exhibited Salon 1882. Britannica (Chabrier) confirms Chabrier bought the painting; 'hung above his piano' not confirmed.

current_text: Cézanne worked seven years on The Large Bathers, unfinished at his death in 1906; Philadelphia paid $110,000 in 1937 and a paper protested that 41,000 citizens had no bathtub.
new_text: Cézanne worked seven years on The Large Bathers, unfinished at his death in 1906; Philadelphia paid $110,000 in 1937 and a paper protested that 41,000 citizens had no bathtub.
source_note: Barnes Foundation 'Battle of the Bathers' page confirms only a 1937 press feud over Philadelphia's acquisition; price and bathtub figure found only in Wikipedia-derived sites.

current_text: Van Gogh shot himself on 27 July 1890, walked back to the Auberge Ravoux, and died in his attic room there in the early hours of 29 July, with Theo at his side.
new_text: Van Gogh shot himself on 27 July 1890, walked back to the Auberge Ravoux, and died in his attic room there in the early hours of 29 July, with Theo at his side.
source_note: Van Gogh Museum: shot himself 27 July 1890 near Auvers, walked back to the Ravoux inn, died 29 July in his attic room with Theo present. 'Early hours' not confirmed.

current_text: Seurat died on 29 March 1891, aged 31, probably of diphtheria, while his unfinished The Circus hung at the Salon des Indépendants; it is now at Orsay.
new_text: Seurat died on 29 March 1891, aged 31, probably of diphtheria, while his unfinished The Circus hung at the Salon des Indépendants; it is now at Orsay.
source_note: Orsay: Le Cirque left unfinished; shown at the 1891 Indépendants; Seurat died of diphtheria days after the Salon opened, aged 31. Britannica confirms death 29 March 1891.

current_text: Signac sailed his 11-metre boat Olympia, named after Manet's painting, and from 1892 based it at the little port of Saint-Tropez, which he is credited with 'discovering'.
new_text: Signac sailed his 11-metre boat Olympia, named after Manet's painting, and from 1892 based it at the little port of Saint-Tropez, which he is credited with 'discovering'.
source_note: Met (2001 Signac exhibition): an enthusiastic sailor, Signac discovered Saint-Tropez aboard his yacht Olympia and settled there in 1892. Boat length (11 m) and naming after Manet's painting not confirmed.

current_text: Durand-Ruel himself nearly went under first: 'Without America, I would have been lost, ruined, after having bought so many Monets and Renoirs. The two exhibitions there in 1886 saved me.'
new_text: Durand-Ruel himself nearly went under first: 'Without America, I would have been lost, ruined, after having bought so many Monets and Renoirs. The two exhibitions there in 1886 saved me.'
source_note: NPR (2015) and Philadelphia Museum confirm the 1886 New York shows (about 300 works) saved him, but the exact quotation was not found in a stronger source.

current_text: The first Impressionist show ran 15 April-15 May 1874 at Nadar's studio, 35 boulevard des Capucines: 30 artists, 165 works, 1 franc entry, about 3,500 visitors.
new_text: The first Impressionist show ran 15 April-15 May 1874 at Nadar's studio, 35 boulevard des Capucines: 30 artists, 165 works, 1 franc entry, about 3,500 visitors.
source_note: National Gallery of Art: opened 15 April 1874 at 35 boulevard des Capucines in Nadar's former studio; 30 artists; about 3,500 visitors in the month. NGA cites some 200 works gathered (165 is the catalogue count); 1 franc entry not confirmed.

current_text: Gauguin reached Arles in late October 1888 and stayed about nine weeks at the Yellow House, leaving after the evening of 23 December, when Vincent cut off his ear.
new_text: Gauguin reached Arles in late October 1888 and stayed about nine weeks at the Yellow House, leaving after the evening of 23 December, when Vincent cut off his ear.
source_note: Van Gogh Museum / Art Institute: Gauguin arrived 23 October 1888, lived at the Yellow House; the collaboration ended abruptly on 23 December 1888 when Vincent injured his ear and Gauguin returned to Paris.

current_text: Atuona sits at about 9°48'S, 139°02'W, on the south coast of Hiva Oa.
new_text: Atuona sits at about 9°48'S, 139°02'W, on the south coast of Hiva Oa.
source_note: A gazetteer-style result gave -9.8009, -139.0324 (consistent), but no authoritative source page could be pinned.

current_text: Mount Temetiu, the island summit at about 1,213 m (sources range up to 1,276 m), towers over Atuona and the western end of the Bay of Traitors.
new_text: Mount Temetiu, the island summit at about 1,213 m (sources range up to 1,276 m), towers over Atuona and the western end of the Bay of Traitors.
source_note: Britannica: slopes rise to some 4,000 feet (1,200 m) at Mount Temetiu; Atuona on the Baie des Traitres. Tahiti Tourisme gives 1,276 m. Exact 1,213 m not confirmed.

current_text: The bay at Atuona, Ta'aoa or the Bay of Traitors, lies inside the crater of the old volcano that built this side of Hiva Oa.
new_text: The bay at Atuona, Ta'aoa or the Bay of Traitors, lies inside the crater of the old volcano that built this side of Hiva Oa.
source_note: Britannica and Tahiti Tourisme confirm Ta'aoa / Bay of Traitors at Atuona and volcanic origin, but not that the bay lies inside a crater.

current_text: Gauguin is buried not in a church but in the hillside Calvary (Calvaire) cemetery above Atuona; he had bought his house plot from the Catholic mission.
new_text: Gauguin is buried not in a church but in the hillside Calvary (Calvaire) cemetery above Atuona; he had bought his house plot from the Catholic mission.
source_note: Britannica: bought a plot in the village centre from the bishop (Catholic mission). Tahiti Tourisme confirms burial in the Calvaire cemetery, Atuona.

current_text: His grave of unhewn pinkish stones in Calvary cemetery looks over Atuona Bay; a bronze cast of his Oviri was set on it on 29 March 1973; Jacques Brel lies a few metres away.
new_text: His grave of unhewn pinkish stones in Calvary cemetery looks over Atuona Bay; a bronze cast of his Oviri was set on it on 29 March 1973; Jacques Brel lies a few metres away.
source_note: Tahiti Tourisme (official tourism board): Gauguin and Brel buried a few metres apart in the Calvaire cemetery, Atuona. The 29 March 1973 bronze Oviri and the stone description not confirmed outside Wikipedia.

current_text: Phillips was founded in London in 1796 by Harry Phillips, formerly a clerk to James Christie; with no staff or premises he held a dozen sales in year one, selling anything from tea services to a saddle mare.
new_text: Phillips was founded in London in 1796 by Harry Phillips, formerly a clerk to James Christie; with no staff or premises he held a dozen sales in year one, selling anything from tea services to a saddle mare.
source_note: Phillips: founded 1796 by Harry Phillips, former senior clerk at 'a well-established London auction house', no staff, no permanent premises, 12 auctions in 12 locations in year one. Christie not named; tea services/saddle mare not mentioned.

current_text: In May 1990 paper magnate Ryoei Saito bought Van Gogh's Portrait of Dr Gachet at Christie's for $82.5M and, two days later, Renoir's Bal du moulin de la Galette for $78.1M; he later joked of cremating them.
new_text: In May 1990 paper magnate Ryoei Saito bought Van Gogh's Portrait of Dr Gachet at Christie's for $82.5M and, two days later, Renoir's Bal du moulin de la Galette for $78.1M; he later joked of cremating them.
source_note: The Art Newspaper (1996): Gachet bought at Christie's in 1990 for $82.5m, Moulin de la Galette for $78.1m; he said he was considering burning both at his cremation, later denied it. 'Two days later' (Renoir at Sotheby's) not stated there.

current_text: December 1865: signed on at Le Havre as a pilot's apprentice on the clipper Luzitano, later second lieutenant on the three-master Chili; 1868 navy service on the corvette Jérôme-Napoléon.
new_text: December 1865: signed on at Le Havre as a pilot's apprentice on the clipper Luzitano, later second lieutenant on the three-master Chili; 1868 navy service on the corvette Jérôme-Napoléon.
source_note: Met and Tate confirm only merchant marine at 17 and navy service; ship names and ranks not found in a stronger source.

current_text: Summer 1886: first stay at Pont-Aven, chosen because it was cheap; an accomplished boxer and fencer, he quickly dominated the young art students there.
new_text: Summer 1886: first stay at Pont-Aven, chosen because it was cheap; an accomplished boxer and fencer, he quickly dominated the young art students there.
source_note: Britannica / NGA: summer 1886 trip to Pont-Aven seeking a simpler, more frugal life. Boxer/fencer and dominance over students not confirmed.

current_text: First Tahiti trip: sailed 1 April 1891, back in France August 1893; painted Spirit of the Dead Watching (Manao tupapau, 1892) on burlap.
new_text: First Tahiti trip: sailed 1 April 1891, back in France August 1893; painted Spirit of the Dead Watching (Manao tupapau, 1892) on burlap.
source_note: Buffalo AKG: Manao tupapau, 1892, oil on burlap (jute) mounted on canvas. Britannica confirms April 1891 departure; a Britannica summary gives his return as July 1893 (he left Tahiti in June; landing in August not confirmed) - check if the month matters.

current_text: Arrived at Atuona, Hiva Oa, on 16 September 1901, and bought land in the town centre from the Catholic mission after first attending mass regularly.
new_text: Arrived at Atuona, Hiva Oa, on 16 September 1901, and bought land in the town centre from the Catholic mission after first attending mass regularly.
source_note: Britannica: moved to Hiva Oa in September 1901 and bought land in the village centre from the bishop. Exact day (16th) and mass attendance not confirmed.

current_text: The Yellow Christ (1889): its Christ copies a 17th-century painted wooden crucifix in the Trémalo chapel near Pont-Aven; now Buffalo AKG Art Museum.
new_text: The Yellow Christ (1889): its Christ copies a 17th-century painted wooden crucifix in the Trémalo chapel near Pont-Aven; now Buffalo AKG Art Museum.
source_note: Buffalo AKG object page: 1889; central figure based on a seventeenth-century painted wooden crucifix in the nearby Trémalo Chapel.

current_text: Mahana no atua (1894, Art Institute of Chicago) was painted in Paris from memory; its idol of the goddess Hina derives from photographs of Borobudur reliefs.
new_text: Mahana no atua (1894, Art Institute of Chicago) was painted in Paris from memory; its idol of the goddess Hina derives from photographs of Borobudur reliefs.
source_note: Art Institute: 1894, produced in Paris after the first Tahiti trip, drawn from fantasy and memory. AIC Gauguin catalogue (publications.artic.edu) on Hina and Gauguin's Borobudur relief photographs; direct Hina-from-Borobudur link for this canvas is via that catalogue.

current_text: Where Do We Come From? (1897-98, MFA Boston) is 139 x 375 cm, about 3.75 m; after finishing it he tried to kill himself with arsenic, months after daughter Aline died.
new_text: Where Do We Come From? (1897-98, MFA Boston) is 139.1 x 374.6 cm, about 3.75 m; after finishing it he tried to kill himself with arsenic, months after daughter Aline died.
source_note: MFA Boston: 1897-98, 139.1 x 374.6 cm, painted during his winter-1897 crisis; Orsay confirms Aline died 1897. The arsenic suicide attempt is not on the MFA page.

current_text: In Martinique (1887) he began setting analogous colours side by side for a muted effect, soon moving to non-representational colour with a life of its own.
new_text: In Martinique (1887) he began setting analogous colours side by side for a muted effect, soon moving to non-representational colour with a life of its own.
source_note: Britannica / Van Gogh Museum confirm Martinique 1887 with Laval and larger unmodulated colour planes, not the 'analogous colours' wording.

current_text: 'Cloisonnism' was coined by critic Édouard Dujardin in the Revue indépendante, March 1888, for Louis Anquetin's paintings; Bernard and Gauguin then worked in the style.
new_text: 'Cloisonnism' was coined by critic Édouard Dujardin in the Revue indépendante, March 1888, for Louis Anquetin's paintings; Bernard and Gauguin then worked in the style.
source_note: Van Gogh Letters scholarly edition (Van Gogh Museum/Huygens): Dujardin, 'Aux XX et aux Indépendants. Le cloisonisme', Revue indépendante, March 1888, on Anquetin. Britannica (Synthetism) confirms Bernard and Gauguin in the style.

current_text: He carved wood from his stockbroker years: a carved and painted mahogany medallion of the singer Valérie Roumi (1880), now in the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek.
new_text: He carved wood from his stockbroker years: a carved and painted mahogany medallion of the singer Valérie Roumi (1880), now in the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek.
source_note: Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek/Fondet record: 'Chanteuse', 1880, mahogany and plaster relief, painted and gilded, 53 cm diameter, inv. M.IN 3230. Sitter's name Valérie Roumi not confirmed there.

current_text: By September 1902 he took morphine injections, then handed his syringe set to a neighbour and used laudanum; an empty laudanum bottle stood by his deathbed.
new_text: By September 1902 he took morphine injections, then handed his syringe set to a neighbour and used laudanum; an empty laudanum bottle stood by his deathbed.
source_note: The Art Newspaper (2007) confirms a syringe and morphine ampoules found in his Atuona well, NGA Australia that he relied on morphine; syringe handover, laudanum and deathbed bottle not found in a stronger source.

current_text: Buried in Atuona's Catholic Calvary Cemetery at 2pm the day after his death; a bronze cast of his Oviri was set on the grave in 1973, as he had wished.
new_text: Buried in Atuona's Catholic Calvary Cemetery at 2pm the day after his death; a bronze cast of his Oviri was set on the grave in 1973, as he had wished.
source_note: Orsay (Oviri): in 1900 he asked for Oviri to put on his tomb. Tahiti Tourisme: buried in the Calvaire cemetery, Atuona. Burial at 2pm next day and 1973 bronze not confirmed outside Wikipedia.

current_text: Tate Modern drew 5.25 million visitors in its first year, double the 2.5 million the three older Tates drew combined; it peaked at 6.1 million in 2019 and recorded about 4.6 million in 2024.
new_text: Tate Modern drew 5.25 million visitors in its first year, double the 2.5 million the three older Tates drew combined; it peaked at 6.1 million in 2019 and recorded about 4.6 million in 2024.
source_note: Tate press release: 5.25 million May 2000-May 2001. The Art Newspaper: record 6.1 million in 2019; ALVA 2024: 4,603,025. Comparison with older Tates (2.5 million combined) not confirmed.

current_text: White Cube is Jay Jopling's gallery, not Hirst's: it opened in May 1993 in one small square room on Duke Street, St James's, and in its first decade never showed the same artist twice. Hirst was among its artists.
new_text: White Cube is Jay Jopling's gallery, not Hirst's: it opened in May 1993 in one small square room on Duke Street, St James's, and in its first decade never showed the same artist twice. Hirst was among its artists.
source_note: White Cube: founded 1993 by Jay Jopling; small white room on Duke Street, St James's; 75 shows by 75 artists 1993-2001, no artist shown twice in the first decade. Opening month (May) not confirmed.

current_text: Philip Johnson's Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden (completed April 1953) set marble-paved terraces around shallow pools; Picasso's She-Goat and Rodin's Monument to Balzac have stood there.
new_text: Philip Johnson's Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden (completed April 1953) set marble-paved terraces around shallow pools; Picasso's She-Goat and Rodin's Monument to Balzac have stood there.
source_note: MoMA: designed 1953 by Philip Johnson as a 'roofless room' with marble-paved areas and fountain pools; She-Goat in the garden. Month (April) not confirmed; Balzac is now in the Agnes Gund Garden Lobby.

current_text: The Broad opened on 20 September 2015 with free general admission; Diller Scofidio + Renfro designed the 120,000-sq-ft building around a 'veil-and-vault' concept.
new_text: The Broad opened on 20 September 2015 with free general admission; Diller Scofidio + Renfro designed the 120,000-sq-ft building around a 'veil-and-vault' concept.
source_note: The Broad press release: opened 20 September 2015, free general admission, designed by Diller Scofidio + Renfro with Gensler, 120,000 sq ft. 'Veil and vault' is in the museum's architectural fact sheet (not re-read here).

current_text: Art Basel was started in 1970 by Basel gallerists Ernst Beyeler, Trudl Bruckner and Balz Hilt; it added Miami Beach (2002), Hong Kong (2013), Paris (2022) and Qatar (2026).
new_text: Art Basel was started in 1970 by Basel gallerists Ernst Beyeler, Trudl Bruckner and Balz Hilt; it added Miami Beach (2002), Hong Kong (2013), Paris (2022) and Qatar (2026).
source_note: Art Basel: founded 1970 by Basel gallerists Trudl Bruckner, Balz Hilt and Ernst Beyeler; Art Basel Qatar debuted Doha, February 2026. Miami/Hong Kong/Paris years per the same history page.

current_text: The Venice Biennale opened on 30 April 1895 in the presence of the Italian King and Queen; Belgium built the first national pavilion in 1907, followed by Germany, Britain and Hungary in 1909.
new_text: The Venice Biennale opened on 30 April 1895 in the presence of the Italian King and Queen; Belgium built the first national pavilion in 1907, followed by Germany, Britain and Hungary in 1909.
source_note: La Biennale: first International Art Exhibition 30 April 1895 (tied to King Umberto and Queen Margherita); Belgium's pavilion the first foreign one, 1907. 1909 pavilions (Germany, Britain, Hungary) not re-checked.

current_text: The YBAs coalesced around Freeze, a July 1988 show Goldsmiths student Damien Hirst organised in an empty Port of London Authority building in Docklands, with Sarah Lucas, Gary Hume and others.
new_text: The YBAs coalesced around Freeze, a July 1988 show Goldsmiths student Damien Hirst organised in an empty Port of London Authority building in Docklands, with Sarah Lucas, Gary Hume and others.
source_note: Tate: Freeze, 1988, organised by Goldsmiths student Damien Hirst in an empty London Port Authority building in Docklands; Sarah Lucas among the artists. Month (July) and Gary Hume not confirmed on this page.

current_text: Beeple's NFT Everydays: The First 5000 Days, a collage of daily images he began on 1 May 2007, sold at Christie's in March 2021 for $69.3 million, paid in Ether.
new_text: Beeple's NFT Everydays: The First 5000 Days, a collage of daily images he began on 1 May 2007, sold at Christie's in March 2021 for $69.3 million, paid in Ether.
source_note: The Art Newspaper / ARTnews: sold at Christie's for $69.3m (about 42,329 Ether, first crypto payment Christie's accepted); daily images from 1 May 2007 to 7 January 2021.
